en: The various metaphorical designations of self and phenomena that occur are indeed the transformation of consciousness; and that transformation is threefold:
maturation, that which is called mentation, and the representation of objects.

Therein, the consciousness called *ālaya* is the maturation (*vipāka*) containing all seeds; it has an imperceptible representation of both appropriation and the [physical] locus, and it is always accompanied by contact, mental attention, feeling, perception, and volition. (2–3)
"In that state, the feeling is equanimity, and it is unobscured-neutral;
likewise, contact and the other [mental factors] are so, and it proceeds like a continuous stream. (4)
And that storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) proceeds as a stream like a torrent, yet it is not a single, indivisible entity.
Demonstrating this point, he says: "And that storehouse-consciousness," and so forth;
this is easily understood.
Demonstrating the nature of a stream (*srotas*), he says: "In that regard, 'stream'... and so forth.
The continuous, uninterrupted progression of cause and effect is called a stream.
Demonstrating the essential nature of a flood (*ogha*), he says: "Of a mass of water... and so forth.
For that continuous flow of water which exists between its preceding and succeeding parts without interruption is called a "current" (*ogha*).
Having thus explained the meaning of the word, he says—"Just as a current," and so forth—in order to demonstrate the meaning of the Sūtra.

Just as a current indeed proceeds while dragging along grass and other such things, even so the *ālayavijñāna*, accompanied by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of meritorious and other types of karma, proceeds in a continuous stream without interruption, dragging along contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors].
Again, another asks: "In that way, by means of the stream," and so forth.
It must be stated at what stage there is the cessation (*vyāvṛtti*) of that storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as it proceeds in such a continuous succession.
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says:
"His cessation occurs at the stage of Arhatship," and so forth;
at the time of attaining Arhatship, his [defilements] cease.
Another, not knowing, asks: "What, then, is arhatship?
The proponent of the established doctrine says: "By connection with which," and so forth.
That dharma through connection with which this living being is called an "Arhat" is what is termed "arhatship."
Not knowing that supreme dharma, he asks: "Of which dharma, moreover," and so forth;
[he asks] "by connection with which dharma is one called an Arhat?
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says: "By the knowledge of destruction," and so forth.
Because of the attainment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), he is called an Arhat.

Why does that storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) cease? To this he says: in that state, whatever corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) was based upon the storehouse-consciousness is abandoned entirely without remainder;
therefore, the storehouse-consciousness becomes ceased.
The meaning is that the basis for the seeds of the afflictions has been removed from it. That state in which the ālayavijñāna ceases is called the state of an Arhat;
for one is designated an Arhat when either the body of liberation (vimuktikāya) or the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is attained.
Thus, the transformation known as maturation (*vipāka*) has been explained in detail;
"with its analysis" (*savibhaṅga*) means "with its full exposition.
Showing the underlying intention regarding the second transformation, he says: "Now, that which is called mentation," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "Depending upon that," and so forth.
He will provide the explanation for this later.
Now, however, demonstrating the connection with the *kārikās*, he says: "In that regard, just as for the visual and other cognitions," and so forth.
While the basis (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*) are well-established for the visual and other cognitions, such establishment does not exist for the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).
It is not logical for it to function independently of a basis and an object.
Therefore, for the purpose of demonstrating its basis and its object, and for the purpose of demonstrating its etymological derivation:
"Depending upon that, it proceeds;
having that as its object, the consciousness called *manas* has the nature of mentation. (5)
He states the verse beginning with these words:

"Depending upon and taking as its object the *ālayavijñāna*, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) functions; and because its nature is that of mentation (*manana*), it is designated as 'mind' (*manas*). This is the meaning of the Sūtra.
He states the explanation of the individual members [of the compound], beginning with "it proceeds depending upon that" (*tat āśritya pravartate*).

The meaning is that here the word "that" (*tacchabdena*) should be connected to the *ālayavijñāna*. To the question, "In what way, then, is this [consciousness] dependent upon the *ālayavijñāna*? he says: "For it has its basis in the latencies thereof" (*tadvāsanāśrayas hi*), and so forth.
Since the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the basis for the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), the afflicted mind proceeds by depending upon the store-consciousness.
The explanation of the term "proceeds" (*pravartate*) is that it arises as a continuum (*santāna*), meaning it arises through the connection of a succession of moments (*kṣaṇaparamparā*).
Providing another explanation for this very point, he says: "Or else, in whichever realm (*dhātu*)... and so forth.

In whichever realm—such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—or in whichever stage (*bhūmi*)—such as the first dhyāna—the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is perceived as maturation (*vipāka*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) also belongs to that same realm or that same stage. Therefore, because its activity is bound to the storehouse consciousness, it is said to "proceed depending upon" it.
Showing its object, he says: "That is its object," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "It has the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its very object," and so forth.

Because the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other [afflictions], it takes the storehouse-consciousness itself as its object through the mode of "I" and "mine."
Anticipating the objection that "the basis itself is the object," he asks: "But how, then... and so forth.
Since the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) arises from that very mind which serves as its basis (*āśraya*), how can that [basis] itself become its object (*ālambana*)?
For the meaning of "object" is one thing, and the meaning of "basis" is another; how, then, can these two be compatible?
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī), establishing an equivalence, says: "Just as for certain [schools] who do not accept that [defiled mind]," and so forth.

For those who do not accept a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), just as in a certain state of self-reflection upon one's own mind immediately after it has ceased, mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) arises from that very mind which serves as its immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); in that same way, that mental consciousness will indeed have its own basis as its object.
Regarding what the name of this consciousness is—which has its own basis as its object—he says: "It is called *manas*, etc.
This is easy to understand.
Having thus explained the meaning of the terms, he speaks—beginning with "that storehouse-consciousness"—in order to demonstrate the meaning of the sūtra.
That consciousness which has been called "mind" (manas) proceeds by depending upon the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and has the storehouse-consciousness as its object.
By this, he shows what is to be excluded by the term "mind."
For, by using the term "mind" (*manas*), he distinguishes it from both the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Asking about its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he says: "What, then, is its intrinsic nature? and so forth.
[The answer is: "It has the nature of mentation (*mananātmaka*)."

Because it constantly conceives "I" and "mine," its intrinsic nature is that of cogitation (*manana*). Providing an etymological derivation for it, [the author] says: "And thus, because its essence consists of cogitation," and so forth.
Since its essence is cogitation, it is called *manas* (mind).

"By the method of etymology" means by the principle of verbal derivation (*nirvacana*). Establishing the connection with the verse, he says: "Because it has the nature of consciousness," and so forth.
This is easily understood.
In order to establish the nature, number, and time of the mental factors (*caitasika*), he says:
"Always accompanied by the four afflictions which are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)," and so forth.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*), which are of an obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.
In order to show what is excluded by the mention of "afflictions," he says: "For these [mental factors]... and so forth.
This is easily understood.
Showing what is to be excluded by the specific number, he says: "The afflictions (*kleśa*) are also six," and so forth.
This too is easily understood.
Since the word *sahita* also denotes one who possesses aesthetic relish (*rasika*), he says: "*Sahitam*," and so forth.
This too is easily understood.

Why is it associated with the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)? To this he says: "For not by the obscured," and so forth. Since the obscured-unspecified is the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), therefore association of the unwholesome (*akuśala*) factors with the obscured consciousness is not tenable; thus he says: "The obscured [are so called] because of being afflicted."

Because they are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), the meaning is that they are "obstructed" (*nivṛta*). If they are obstructed, why are they called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*)? To this he says: "indeterminate," and so forth.
Because they are not defined (*vyākriyante*) as either wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*), they are therefore called indeterminate.
Showing the timing of this, he says: "always," and so forth.
As long as the afflicted mind exists, it is associated with those [afflictions] at all times.
Establishing the connection with the verse, he says: "because of the general indication," and so forth.
The general statement "by four afflictions" has been made, but it is not understood specifically which four they are. Therefore, showing them in detail, he says:
"By those known as self-view, self-delusion, self-pride, and self-love. (6)
And so forth.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that [the self-view arises] through these four: by means of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), delusion regarding the self (*ātmamoha*), and attachment to the self (*ātmasneha*).
To demonstrate the view of self and the others, he says: "In the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandheṣu*)," and so forth.

The grasping at a self within the five aggregates of clinging is what is here termed "the view of self" (ātmadṛṣṭi). He shows this very same thing by means of its well-known synonym, "the view of a real body" (satkāyadṛṣṭi). Ignorance is expressed by the word "delusion" (moha).
Delusion regarding the self is *ātmamoha*.
That which arises as pride (*māna*) toward the self is called *ātmamāna*.
He shows this very [term] by means of a well-known synonym: "pride in this [self]" (*asmin mānaḥ*).
The affection that arises toward the self is called "self-love" (*ātmasneha*).
By the term "love for the self" (*ātmaprema*), he shows its well-known synonym.

How is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) the object of these [afflictions]? To this he says: "In that regard, there is delusion concerning the nature of the storehouse-consciousness," and so forth.
For one who does not know the nature of the storehouse-consciousness as being impermanent and so on, forms a grasping for a self toward it.
That ignorance which consists in the thought, "This is mine; this is my self," is self-delusion (*ātmamoha*).
That which is the grasping at a self is the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
And following the time of the vision of a self, that inflation of the mind which arises by the power of the nature of things is called the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
When these three—the triad beginning with delusion—are present, the attachment that subsequently arises toward the object conceived as a self is called self-love (*ātmasneha*).
He states a verse summarizing the meaning already explained: "And it says," and so forth.
The meaning of the verse is that the mind, which is characterized by mentation (*manana*), is afflicted by the four afflictions (*kleśa*) beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Afflicted" (*saṃkliṣṭa*) means made impure (*malinīkṛta*).
By means of the second verse, demonstrating the logical proof for the existence of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), he says: "But the cause of error," and so forth.
Since the afflicted mind is at all times the cause of error, it must be understood that it exists.
To which error? He says: "In a wholesome or neutral state of consciousness," and so forth.
In a state of wholesome mind, the mark of the *ahaṃkāra* is such as "I give a gift" and so forth;
in a state of neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind, the mark of the *ahaṃkāra* is such as "I cut leaves.
Therefore, it is said that the mark is that which constitutes the misconception of self (*ātmaviparyāsa*) with respect to the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is not the self.
Establishing the connection with the *kārikā*, he says: "For these, beginning with self-delusion (*ātmamoha*)... and so forth.
Here, the nine stages (*bhūmi*) should be understood as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
The remainder is easily understood.
To dispel doubt, he says:
"In whatever [place] one is born, by that [place] one is permeated," and so forth.
He explains this with the words beginning "wherever born" (*yatra jātaḥ*), and so forth.

In whichever realm (*dhātu*) or stage (*bhūmi*) a living being is born, he is associated only with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other [afflictions] belonging to that realm and that stage, not with those belonging to another realm or another stage.
Showing the Sūtra, he says: "But why [is it] by four alone? and so forth.
This is easily understood.
The author of the Bhāṣya says: "He says 'no'," and so forth. Explaining this, he says:
"And by other [contacts] such as touch," and so forth;
this too is easily understood.
He shows the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) with the words "the word 'and'... and so forth.

And thus, it is stated by the phrase "with touch (*sparśa*) and so forth" that the mind is not only associated with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the like, but is also associated with others such as touch.
He shows the meaning of the word "initial" (*ādya*) with the words: "those which exist at the beginning are the initial ones."
What, then, is the reason that these are associated with contact (*sparśa*) and the others? He says: "For these five factors," and so forth.

Since these five factors, beginning with contact, are held to be omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), they are therefore associated with all consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). Demonstrating the restriction (*niyama*) regarding their realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*), he says: "By these also," and so forth.
The meaning of this has already been explained.
Providing another explanation on this very point, he says: "If that mind is afflicted," and so forth;
or else, "by others," and so forth.

The phrase "by other [factors] such as contact" is stated for the purpose of distinguishing [the afflicted mind] from those factors such as contact that are associated with the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

For it is held that in the root-consciousness (mūlavijñāna), contact and the other factors are unobscured-indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta); however, in the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas), they are obscured-indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta), just like the mind itself. Establishing the connection with the Sūtra, he says: "If that afflicted mind," and so forth.
If the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) were to function without distinction throughout all states—whether afflicted or neutral—it would follow that there is no cessation of it.
As long as it does not cease, how could there be liberation?
Therefore, it follows that liberation would be impossible for living beings.
The proponent of the established doctrine says: "It does not follow," and so forth.
It does not follow that there is an absence of liberation, because—that [non-existence] does not belong to the Arhat.
It does not exist in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), nor in the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*).

The afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) of an Arhat does not exist during the state of the attainment of cessation, nor does it exist in the supramundane path; it is abandoned by that which is called the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
Thus, the afflicted mind is abandoned entirely and completely by that very same uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*).
And therefore, just as the afflictions do not exist for an Arhat, so too they do not exist at that time [for the Anāgāmin].
Now, he asks why they do not exist for an Anāgāmin, and says: "Even for one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness," and so forth.

Indeed, for an Anāgāmin who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness and has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) does not exist during the state of the absorption of cessation.
Since the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is obtained through the power of the path (*mārga*), it does not exist there even for that brief duration, just as the path itself does not.
Now, [the author] asks: "From where does that [consciousness] arise for one who has emerged from it? and replies with the words "And from cessation," etc.
When one has emerged from the attainment of cessation, it arises again precisely from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
For he possesses latent impressions (*vāsanā*) therein.
Demonstrating the absence [of such impressions] for one who stands on the path, he says: "On the path, it becomes supramundane (*lokottara*). This has already been explained in meaning.
But surely it should have been stated simply as "and not on the path"; for what purpose was the term "supramundane" (lokottara) employed?
He replies: "The inclusion of the supramundane is for the sake of distinguishing [it] from the mundane.
This is easy to understand.
To the question "For what purpose is the mundane [path] excluded?", he says: "But in the mundane," and so forth.
The word *tu* (but) has the sense of "because.

Because the activity of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is indeed accepted in the mundane path, why does it not operate in the supramundane? To this he says: "Of the vision of selflessness," and so forth.

Since the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya-darśana*) is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is unable to function within the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*).
For the adverse element (*vipakṣa*) and its antidote do not exist simultaneously.
Consequently, due to the absence of simultaneity between the adverse element and its antidote, the afflicted mind does not function for that duration within the supramundane path.
But when one has emerged from the supramundane path, it then arises again from the *ālayavijñāna* itself. Summarizing, he says: "This is the second transformation."
"Thus, etc.
means that what was previously mentioned is now being explained.
Showing the connection with the third transformation, he says: "Immediately after the second transformation," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
To the question "Which one is it?", he says: "That which belongs to the third [category] of the sixfold."
"The apprehension of the object, that is [the third transformation]," and so forth.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that the apprehension of the sixfold object is the third transformation of consciousness.
In this context, the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*) must be explained.

Since the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the comprehension of the meanings of its constituent words, he says "of the sixfold," etc., while demonstrating the meaning of the words;
this is easily understood.
With the words "That, moreover," and so forth, he asks about its divisions.
The proponent of the established tenets (siddhāntavādī), demonstrating the divisions, says:
"It is wholesome, unwholesome, and non-dual. (8)
Thus, explaining this, he says: "wholesome," and so forth.
By the mention of "non-dual," the indeterminate is expressed.
The remainder is easily understood.
Showing the essential nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth, he says: "By non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion," and so on.
Furthermore, being in doubt regarding the nature of these mental factors (*caitasika*) and their number, he asks: "But by what kind [of factors]? and so forth.

Dispelling two doubts, he says: "Associated with the omnipresent, the specific, and the wholesome mental factors, as well as with the afflictions and the secondary afflictions, it [the mind] possesses the three types of feeling. (9)
And so forth.
"It is associated with the universal [factors] and so on" is the concise meaning of the sūtra.
Furthermore, one who is still in doubt regarding the universal factors and so on asks: "As for these... and so forth.
This is self-evident.
To demonstrate that, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says:
"The first [sensations] are touch and so forth."
The "pervasive" (sarvatraga) factors are intended [here]. Why are they called "the first pervasive ones"? To this he says: "They are called 'first' because they were taught at the beginning.
Explaining this, he says: "For instance, the pervasive ones," and so forth.
Since the universal factors (*sarvatraga*) were mentioned first in the immediately preceding verse, they are called "the first.
As for those who provide the explanation that "contact and the others are the first," they explain what is utterly irrelevant;
for in the immediately preceding verse, the universal factors were mentioned at the beginning, not contact and the others.
Regarding the phrase "contact and so forth" (*sparśādayaḥ*), he provides the compound analysis by saying: "contact is the first among these," and so on.
This has already been explained.
Now, as to why these are called "omnipresent" (sarvatraga), he says: "Furthermore, those... and so forth.
Because these [factors], such as contact (sparśa) and the rest, follow after every state of mind, they are therefore called omnipresent.
How is this known? To this he says: "In that way, in the root-consciousness (mūlavijñāna)... and so forth.
Since they also exist in the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), it is established that they accompany all states of mind.

By the phrase "with reference to the specific mental factors (*viniyata*)," he demonstrates the connection with the verse. [The verse says: "Desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*) together..."
By the words "determined by concentration and wisdom," and so forth, he shows the specific mental factors (*viniyata*).
The meaning of the Sūtra is that the five beginning with desire (*chanda*) are the specific mental factors.
Why are these called "the determined" (*viniyata*)? He says: "Because of the distinction," and so forth.
Since these are said to be determined with respect to a specific [object], for their object is indeed the specific, not everything.
"What is this so-called *chanda*? he asks, and replies: "In that regard, *chanda*," and so forth. *Chanda* is the desire for an intended object.
By the inclusion of the term "intended" (*abhipreta*), it is made known that [desire] has a specific, determined object.
Since desire does not arise for what is undesired, he asks, "What, then, is desired? and says: "Seeing [the truth], etc.
This is easy to understand.
Showing a synonym for *chanda*, he says: "In that regard, 'vision' (*darśana*), etc.
The conformity to reality (*yathārthatā*) of vision, hearing, and so forth is called both *chanda* and *abhilāṣa* (desire).
Showing its function (*karman*), he says: "And that is the undertaking of vigor (*vīryārambha*), etc."
The meaning is that its function is to become the causal basis for the undertaking of vigor.
Now, as to what this "resolute conviction" (adhimokṣa) is, he says: "Resolute conviction is that which is certain," and so forth.
The concise meaning is that resolute conviction is the firm belief (saṃpratyaya) regarding an object perceived through a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
To the question, "For what purpose is the inclusion of the term 'certain' (niścita)? he replies: "The inclusion of the term 'certain,' etc."
This is easily understood.
To the question "What is this 'ascertained'?", he says: "By means of reasoning," and so forth.
That object which has been rendered free from doubt by means of perception, inference, or authoritative scripture is called "ascertained."

The mental placement of that object in the mind by means of exactly that aspect—such as impermanence and so forth—by which it was determined, and the ascertainment that "it is thus and not otherwise," is called resolve (*adhimokṣa*). Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this [resolve]... and so forth.
The meaning is that his "activity" (*karma*) consists in not being led away from his own established tenets (*svasiddhānta*).
To the question, "In what way is this his activity?", he says: "For one who is preeminent in resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)," and so forth.
Because one who is preeminent in resolute conviction cannot be led away from his own tenets by opponents (*paravādin*), therefore this is his activity.
Now, as to what this mindfulness (*smṛti*) is, he says: "Mindfulness is [the non-forgetting] of a familiar object," and so forth.
Mindfulness is that which is the non-departure from the mind of an object previously experienced, and its bringing back to presence; therefore, it is called mindfulness.
To the question, "What is this so-called 'familiar'?", he says: "A familiar object," and so forth.
This is easily understood.
To the question "Why is mindfulness (smṛti) called non-forgetfulness (apramoṣa)? he says: "Of the object," and so forth.
Since mindfulness is the cause for the non-disappearance of that previous grasping of the object which had occurred, it is therefore called non-forgetfulness.
And thus, because it is the cause of non-disappearance, it is called "non-forgetfulness" (*asaṃpramoṣa*).
Showing its essential nature as verbal expression, he says: "of that which was previously grasped," and so forth.
That which was previously grasped is an object; the recollection of its objective aspect (*ālambanākāra*) is what constitutes this "verbal expressiveness" (*abhilapanatā*).
Showing that the suffix *bhāva* is used in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*), he says: "mere verbalization," and so forth; this is easy to understand.
Showing its object (*karman*), he says: "that, moreover," and so forth; its function (*karman*) is the distraction of the focal object (*ālambana*).

Since, when the object of the mind is repeatedly brought to mind, there is no distraction of the mind toward another object or another aspect, mindfulness is therefore said to have non-distraction as its function. To the question "What is this concentration? he says: "Concentration is [the state] regarding that which is to be examined," and so forth.
The one-pointedness of the mind toward an object that is to be examined is *samādhi*.
By what aspect is it to be examined? To this he says: "the object to be examined," and so forth.
It is to be examined either by way of its qualities (*guṇataḥ*) or by way of its faults (*doṣataḥ*).

The truths of cessation and the path are to be examined in terms of their qualities through aspects such as "peaceful" and "excellent," while the truths of suffering and its origin are to be examined in terms of their defects through aspects such as "impermanent.
That state of having a single object within this [process] is called one-pointedness.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "the support for knowledge," and so forth.
Its function is the attainment of the state of being a cause for knowledge, because when the mind is concentrated, knowledge of things as they truly are (yathābhūtaprajñāna) arises.
To the question "What is this wisdom (dhī)? he says: "Wisdom is prajñā.
Explaining this, he says: "That too is to be examined," and so forth.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that discernment (*pravicaya*) which, regarding an object precisely to be examined, is either applied through yoga, not applied through yoga, or otherwise.
While providing an etymological derivation, he says: "it discerns" (*pravicinoti*), and so forth.
To demonstrate the meaning of discernment, he says: "as if among mixed specific and general characteristics," and so forth.
Discernment (*pravicaya*) is the correct or false understanding of the ripening [of karma] regarding phenomena whose specific and general characteristics appear as if they were intermingled.
To the question, "What, then, is that which is established by reasoning (*yoga-vihita*)?", he says: "Reasoning (*yukti*) is *yoga*.
By the word *yoga*, it is reasoning that is denoted.
Showing that very [definition] through its divisions, he says: "Furthermore, that authoritative instruction," and so forth. This is easily understood.
Showing the meaning of what has been prescribed, he says: "By that threefold [means]," and so forth.
That discernment which is produced regarding the object to be examined is called "prescribed by yoga."
Showing its divisions, he says: "That, moreover, consists of what is derived from hearing," and so forth;
this is easily understood.
Showing the essential nature of that which is derived from hearing and the others, he says: "In that regard, [it is] the word of a reliable person," and so forth.

The understanding that arises by taking the word of a reliable authority as the means of valid cognition is called "consisting of hearing" (*śrutamaya*). That which arises for those who investigate through reasoning is called "consisting of reflection" (*cintāmaya*).
That which arises through the power of meditative concentration is called "consisting of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmaya*).
A person who has become an authority is called an *āpta* (a reliable person).
*Nidhyāna* means thorough investigation.
Showing the divisions of non-application (*ayoga*), he says: "Non-application," and so forth.
Concentration (*samādhi*) that is incorrectly practiced is called "wrongly directed" (*mithyāpraṇihita*).
The remainder is easily understood.
Showing the meaning of what has been prescribed, he says: "By that non-application," and so forth; this has already been explained.
Showing the third mode, he says: "That which is acquired at birth," and so forth.

That understanding of the meaning of things through wisdom accompanied by reflection, as well as that understanding of worldly transactions such as buying and selling, is said to be neither produced by yoga nor produced by non-yoga.

"Obtained through birth" (*upapattipratilambhika*) means that its acquisition occurs through birth; because it possesses this [acquisition], it is "obtained through birth," which signifies being innate (*sahaja*).
"Produced" (*vihita*) means generated or brought about.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
Its function is the removal of doubt;
for one who discerns phenomena through wisdom attains certainty regarding them.
And from the attainment of certainty, doubt is dispelled.
To address whether these arise together or individually, he says: "For these five factors," and so forth.
These five factors also exist even when mutually distinguished from one another.
The meaning is "not necessarily together.
And thus, in whichever mind there is resolve (*adhimokṣa*), it does not necessarily have to be accompanied by the others.
The same should be stated for the other [mental factors] as well.
By means of grasping what is intended, what is determined, what is familiar, and what is examined, it is made known that these [mental factors] have specific objects.
For instance, there is no desire (*chanda*) toward what is not intended,
and there is no resolve (*adhimokṣa*) toward what is not determined.
In that which is unfamiliar, there is no mindfulness;
in that which is not investigated, there is an absence of concentration and wisdom.
Some, however, read this passage differently.
Indeed, these five factors do not exist apart from one another;
and wherever there is resolve (*adhimokṣa*), the others must necessarily be present as well.
Thus they recite it erroneously.
For when desire arises toward a future object, at that time there is no mindfulness (*smṛti*) regarding it, because mindfulness has as its domain only that which has been previously experienced.

And when interest (*chanda*) and so forth arise toward an object that is not being investigated, at that time there is no concentration (*samādhi*) regarding it, because concentration has as its domain only the object currently under investigation.
Or, when desire and the other [mental factors] arise with respect to an unascertained object, there is no resolve (*adhimokṣa*) therein, because its domain is an ascertained object.
Consequently, how could they not exist as distinct from one another?
Demonstrating the connection with what is to be said next, he says: "The specific [factors] have been explained," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
Showing this, he says:
"Faith, as well as shame and dread of blame. (10)
The triad beginning with non-attachment, vigor, serenity accompanied by vigilance,
non-harming, and so forth— these are the wholesome [factors].
Showing their number, he says: "These are eleven," and so forth;
this is easily understood.
Showing the nature of faith (*śraddhā*), he says: "In that regard, faith," and so forth.

Faith (*śraddhā*) is that conviction, clarity, and aspiration regarding wholesome and unwholesome actions, their desirable and undesirable fruits such as suffering, the Truths, and the Jewels beginning with the Perfectly Awakened One.
For faith indeed functions in three ways.
Demonstrating the distinction between the objects of conviction and the other [aspects], he says: "When there is one who possesses qualities," and so forth.
Faith (*śraddhā*) is the mental aspect of conviction regarding the existence of any object that exists, whether it possesses qualities or lacks them;
furthermore, regarding an object that exists and possesses qualities, it is the aspect of serene clarity (*prasāda*);
and regarding an object that exists, possesses qualities, and is capable of being attained or produced, it is the aspect of aspiration (*abhilāṣa*).
Showing the nature of serenity (*prasāda*), he says: "Serenity of the mind," and so forth.

Because faith is incompatible with the turbidity of the mind, when there is association with it, the mind becomes serene by relying on faith through the removal of the stains and turbidity known as the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); therefore, it is called the serenity of the mind.
By the term "turbidity of the mind," the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions are meant.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "Furthermore, it is desire," and so forth.
Its function is to produce the longing for engagement.
For one who has gained conviction regarding a feasible object produces desire, which is the arising of longing for engagement.
Showing the essential nature of *hrī* (moral shame), he says: "Shame," and so forth.
That sense of shame which arises in one who regards oneself and the Dharma regarding a blameworthy act is called *hrī*.
To the question, "What then is the blameless? he says: "Because it is censured by the virtuous," and so forth.

Since that which is censured by the virtuous and which produces undesirable results— namely, evil itself— is called *avadya* (blameworthy), the contraction of the mind that arises when such a blameworthy act has been committed is *lajjā* (shame); and that very same [contraction] is called *hrī* (moral dread).
Showing its function, he says: "And this," and so forth;
the meaning is that its function is the prevention of misconduct.
Showing the essential nature of moral dread (*apatrāpya*), he says: "Moral dread," and so forth.
That which is shame regarding a fault out of regard for the world is *apatrāpya*.
Because this [fault] is censured in the world, and thinking, "The world, knowing me to be a doer of such an act, will censure me," one feels shame regarding the fault out of fear of ill-repute.
Censure (*garhā*) means blame (*nindā*); ill-repute (*akīrti*) is expressed by the word "infamy" (*aśloka*).
Noting that *aślīla* should be read [here],
he says "this too," etc., demonstrating his action;
this has already been explained.
He asks, "What is non-greed? and says: "Non-greed," and so forth.
That dharma which has greed as its opposite is here called non-greed.
He asks, "What is greed? and says: "Greed," and so forth.
Attachment and longing for cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and the requisites of cyclic existence is greed (*lobha*). Its opposite is non-greed (*alobha*).

Therefore, it is said that non-greed is the lack of attachment, the turning away from, the absence of desire, and the absence of longing for cyclic existence and its requisites, such as elephants, horses, and so forth.
He explains non-hatred (*adveṣa*) with the words "non-hatred," and so forth.
Non-hatred is a dharma whose intrinsic nature is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), acting as the antidote to hatred.
He asks, "What, first of all, is hatred? and answers with the words "for hatred," and so forth.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is the malice directed toward sentient beings who cause harm, as well as toward suffering and the causes of suffering, such as poison, thorns, and the like.

Non-hatred (*adveṣa*), however, because it is the antidote to hatred, should be understood as having the nature of being free from malice toward sentient beings, suffering, and the causes of suffering.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "This also," and so forth.
The meaning of this has already been explained.
Demonstrating non-delusion (*amoha*), he says: "Non-delusion," and so forth.
Non-delusion here is that dharma which has the nature of awakening to things as they truly are (*yathābhūtāvabodha*), being the antidote to delusion (*moha*).
First, he asks what delusion itself is: "Delusion" refers to [ignorance] regarding the fruit of action (*karmaphala*), and so forth.
Ignorance regarding karma and so forth is delusion (*moha*).
Non-delusion (*amoha*), however, because it is the antidote to that, should be understood as having the nature of correct comprehension regarding the truths and so forth.
He demonstrates its function with the words "This too," and so on; the meaning of this has already been explained.
He states the essential nature of vigor (*vīrya*) with the words "vigor," and so forth.
Vigor is that enthusiasm of the mind toward wholesome action which serves as the antidote to laziness (*kausīdya*); it does not apply to afflicted action.
Furthermore, that enthusiasm for afflicted action is merely laziness because of its contemptible nature; it is not vigor.
Because one sinks into a contemptible object, that too is indeed *kausīdya* (indolence).
Consequently, there are two kinds of *kausīdya*: that characterized by laziness and afflicted enthusiasm (*utsāha*).
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
Its function is the fulfillment and the perfection of the side of wholesome qualities. To the question "What is pliancy? he says: "Pliancy," and so forth.
Pliancy is that serviceability (*karmanyatā*) of body and mind which serves as the antidote to inner rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*).
"What is this 'dauṣṭhulya'? he asks, and says: "Dauṣṭhulya," and so forth.
The unserviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) of body, speech, and mind is called *dauṣṭhulya*.
Alternatively, *dauṣṭhulya* is the seed (*bīja*) of the defiled phenomena (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*).
To the question "Whence is this [known]? he says: "Upon its departure," and so forth.
Since *prasrabdhi* (pliancy) arises when the seeds of the defiled factors (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*) have departed, therefore that [seed] is also *dauṣṭhulya* (rigidity).
Now, as to what this "adaptability of the body" (*kāya-karmaṇyatā*) is, he says: "In that regard, adaptability of the body," and so forth.
That from which the body’s lightness in its own activities arises is called bodily pliancy (*kāyakarmaṇyatā*).
"Lightness in arising" means agility.
Demonstrating mental pliancy (*cittakarmaṇyatā*), he says: "mental pliancy," and so forth.

For the yogin who is engaged in correct mental attention (*samyag-manasikāra*), that mental factor which is a distinct dharma and serves as the cause for the joy and lightness of his mind is "adaptability of mind" (*citta-karmaṇyatā*).
Joy is bliss (*sukha*); lightness is agility (*pāṭava*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of its association with which the mind... and so forth.
Since the mind proceeds toward its object through association with that mental factor (caitasika dharma), it is therefore called "mental flexibility" (cittakarmanyatā).

If it is the case that there is a distinct mental factor (caitasika-dharmāntara) here called "pliancy" (praśrabdhi), what then is this "bodily pliancy" (kāyapraśrabdhi)? To this he says: "Furthermore, of the body," and so forth.
It should be understood that bodily pliancy is a certain specific tangible object (spraṣṭavya-viśeṣa) of the body itself, which has been drawn forth by joy (prīti).
Why is this so? He says: "Of one whose mind is joyful," and so forth.
For it is stated in a sutra that "when the mind becomes gladdened, then the body becomes pliant.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this [pliancy] occurs by its power," and so forth.
Since the transformation of the basis occurs by the power of pliancy, therefore its function is the extraction of the entire obscuration of afflictions.
Explaining the phrase "she is not negligent," he says: "She is not negligent," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
Since her essential nature is not known through mere etymological derivation alone, he asks: "Who, then, is she? and so forth.
The proponent of the established doctrine says: "Equanimity.
The meaning is that here equanimity is intended to be non-negligent.
Questioning the reason for this, the opponent asks: "Whence is this?"
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī), demonstrating the reason, says: "Because it is exclusively wholesome," and so forth.

Since equanimity (upekṣā) is exclusively wholesome, and all wholesome mental factors (caitasika) are intended to be explained here, yet no direct mention has been made of this [equanimity] as was done for faith (śraddhā) and the others.
Furthermore, no other wholesome mental factors exist apart from the eleven wholesome mental factors;
therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is *upekṣā* alone that is designated by the term "accompanied by heedfulness" (*sāpramādika*).
This is what is meant: in every respect, all eleven wholesome factors are accompanied by *upekṣā*.
In that context, ten [factors] have been explained by way of specific designation (*śṛṅgagrāhika*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) has not been mentioned here by its own name; therefore, it is precisely that which is expressed here by the term "non-negligence" (*sāpramādika*).
What, then, is heedfulness (*apramāda*)? He says: "In that regard, heedfulness," and so forth.
Explaining this very point, he says: "Those [qualities] such as non-attachment," and so forth.

Whatever qualities such as non-attachment one relies upon to abandon unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*) and to cultivate wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*) which serve as the antidotes to unwholesome states—those [qualities], such as non-attachment and the rest, are designated by the term "heedfulness."
For this very reason, it is the antidote to negligence (*pramāda*), because negligence is the opposite of this; and its opposition will be explained later.
Showing its function, he says: "Furthermore, that... and so forth.
The fulfillment of the abundance of all mundane and supramundane qualities is its function.
To the question "What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?", it is said: "Equanimity is evenness of mind," and so forth.

Equanimity is that evenness of mind resulting from the departure of lethargy and excitement; it is the spontaneous flow of the mind without effort; and it is the effortless state of the mind for one who does not apply directed attention (*ābhoga*) toward the mental orientations that inspire joy or spiritual urgency, which are the antidotes to lethargy and excitement.
Furthermore, he asks, "What is the purpose of these many words? and says: "By these three words," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
Then, he asks, "What is this equanimity of mind (cittasamatā)? and says: "In that regard, laxity and excitement," and so forth.
When the mind is either sluggish or excited, it is said to be "uneven.
Because of the absence of sluggishness and excitement, when the mind is initially neither sluggish nor excited, it is then called "evenness.
Thus, this is the evenness of mind.
Demonstrating the state of mental serenity (*cittapraśaṭhatā*), he says: "Then, by way of non-application" (*tato 'nabhisaṃskāreṇa*), and so forth.

Following the attainment of mental equanimity (*cittasamatā*), that continued flow of the concentrated mind which is naturally even—without any effort and in accordance with yoga—is what constitutes the serenity of the mind.
Furthermore, in that state, the yogin has no apprehension regarding dullness (*laya*) or agitation (*auddhatya*) after the attainment of equanimity.
The thought that "this wicked-souled woman will become so again" is of such a nature;
for she has only now reached this state of equilibrium and has not practiced it for a long time.
Therefore, there is room for suspicion.
Demonstrating the effortless nature of the mind, he says: "Then, cultivation," and so forth.
Thereafter, when that cultivation has reached its culmination, because sinking (*laya*) and excitement (*auddhatya*)—its two adversaries—have been distanced, no apprehension regarding them arises.
Consequently, the yogin does not apply effort toward the signs that counteract sinking and excitement, nor toward the mental orientations (*manaskāra*) intended to inspire joy or spiritual urgency.
The state of a yogin whose mind abides in non-effort (*anābhoga*) without performing any mental application (*ābhoga*) is called "the non-effort of the mind.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
Its function is to provide a basis for the non-occurrence of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
"What is non-violence? he asks, and says: "Non-violence," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "By means of killing, binding, and so forth," and so forth.
Non-violence is defined as the non-affliction and non-harming of sentient beings by means of causes of injury such as killing, binding, and the like.
And that [compassion] obstructs the happiness derived from compassion toward sentient beings.
Demonstrating its etymology, he says: "What does it obstruct? and so forth.
By the word *kaṃ*, happiness is expressed.
And thus, it is said that "it obstructs happiness.
To "obstruct" means to conceal.
How is this known?
Because the compassionate person suffers when others suffer, he suppresses his own pleasure through compassion.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
Its function is the non-harming of sentient beings.
Establishing the connection with what is about to be said, he says: "The eleven have been stated," and so forth. This has already been explained. Showing the afflictions (*kleśa*), he says:
The afflictions (kleśa) are attachment, aversion, and delusion; pride, views, and doubt, and so forth. 11.11ab.
Showing the compound, he says: "And passion," and so forth. This has already been explained.
To the question "What is passion? he says: "In that regard, passion," and so forth.

That which is attachment toward existence and enjoyments, as well as the longing for them, is called *rāga* (passion). Attachment refers to clinging toward present objects, while longing refers to desire for future ones. He asks, "What is *pratigha* (hostility)? and replies: "Hostility toward sentient beings," and so forth.

That which is malice toward sentient beings, that harshness of mind toward sentient beings, and that state possessed by which one contemplates harm such as killing or binding for sentient beings—that is *pratigha* (hostility).
Showing its function, he says: "Furthermore, it is... and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "Contact is pleasure," and so forth.
This is easily understood.
How is this known? To this he says: "of one whose mind is full of malice," and so forth.
Because for one whose mind is hostile, suffering and mental distress necessarily manifest.
Because of the manifestation of that [affliction], the mind is tormented;
and when the mind is tormented, because it conforms to it, the body also becomes tormented.
Consequently, in all his modes of conduct, his dwelling is accompanied by suffering and distress.
Dwelling (*vihāra*) means abiding.
And for one whose mind is obstructed, no misconduct is far from him;
therefore, this is called action (*karman*) as it has been described.
To the question "What is delusion? he says: "Delusion is [regarding] the states of woe," and so forth.
That which is ignorance regarding the states of woe and the like is delusion;
it is the non-perverted [view] concerning the relationship between cause and effect.
The non-perversion [of knowledge] consists in the fact that the fruit of the auspicious is desired and the fruit of the inauspicious is undesired.
Demonstrating this action, he says: "And this," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "In that regard, consisting of afflictions, karma, and birth," and so forth.
Defilement is threefold: consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), consisting of karma, and consisting of birth.
It is stated that the acquisition of self-nature—the arising—of each subsequent defilement occurs due to the cause of each preceding defilement among these three types.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this very [defilement] provides the support for such arising.
Because affliction, such as false knowledge and so forth, proceeds only for one who is deluded, and not for one who is undeluded.
To the question "What is the mental [defilement]? he says: "The mental," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "For the mental," and so forth.
Indeed, every mental [defilement] proceeds by depending upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Its intrinsic nature, however, is the quality of being an elevation of the mind; it has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its basis.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "For [it is] in the manner of 'self' and 'mine'," and so forth.

Because one superimposes the notions of "self" and "mine" onto the aggregates (*skandhas*) and, through such distinctions as "I am," "I am thus," "I am learned," or "this sovereignty over phenomena is mine alone," exalts oneself and considers oneself superior to others;
therefore, it is called the mental basis for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And that is disrespect," and so forth.
Its function is to provide a basis for the arising of suffering in one who lacks respect.
What is this lack of respect? He says: "Lack of respect toward those who are venerable," and so forth.

That which is stiffness toward teachers and other venerable persons, as well as toward other individuals possessed of virtuous qualities—that is a lack of respect, characterized by the lack of suppleness in body and speech.
"Stiffness" means a lack of inclination toward prostration.
"Lack of courtesy" means not rising from one's seat with the body or not offering words of welcome and the like.
To the question "What is this arising of suffering?", he says: "Furthermore, the arising of suffering," and so forth.
The arising of another birth is intended here as the arising of suffering.
Demonstrating its divisions, he says: "Furthermore, that is the inflation of the mind," and so forth.
Although the essential nature of the inflation of the mind does not differ, it is nevertheless divided into seven types according to the difference in its causes.
He demonstrates that classification by means of the passage beginning with "māna" (conceit) and "atimāna" (excessive conceit).
To the question "What is *māna*?", he says: "On account of [inferior] family, knowledge, wealth, and so forth," and so on.
The inflation of the mind thinking, "I am superior to one who is inferior in terms of family," or "I am equal to one who is equal in terms of family and so forth"—this is *māna*.

Excessive pride (*atimāna*) is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior to those who are my equals in terms of lineage and so forth, but am better than them in terms of renunciation, moral conduct, and so forth," or "I am equal to those who are superior to me in terms of lineage and so forth, but am my equal in terms of knowledge, wealth, and so forth. Pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*) is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I alone am superior even to those who are superior to me in terms of lineage and so forth, and am my equal in terms of knowledge, wealth, and so forth."
And these three are also based on real entities (*vastuka*);
for they proceed only with respect to existing things such as family and so forth.
Otherwise, they would not be distinguished from false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
The distinction is this: only one person exalts himself by comparison with those inferior to him, a second by comparison with those equal to him, and a third by comparison with those superior to him.
Here, by the word *vijñāna* (knowledge/skill), proficiency in arts such as painting and the like is meant;
by the word *vitta* (wealth), material property is meant.
"Self-conceit," and so forth.

Although the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*) are in reality devoid of a self or what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya*), that inflation of the mind which arises from the persistent attachment to a self and what belongs to a self is called self-conceit (*asmimāna*). As for "inferiority-conceit" (*ūnamāna*), he says: "Inferiority-conceit," and so forth.

When, despite being far inferior in terms of lineage and other qualities, an inflation of mind arises such that one thinks, "I am only slightly inferior in terms of lineage and other qualities," this is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority-complex).
As for what *mithyāmāna* (false pride) is, he says: "False pride," and so forth.
When, while being devoid of virtues, an inflation of mind arises such that one thinks, "I possess virtues," that is *mithyāmāna*.

To the question, "Why is this person one of false pride? he says: "For [he is] devoid of virtues," and so forth. Here, "vices" refers to immorality and the like. A person in whom these exist is one who possesses vices (an *aguṇavān*).

Furthermore, because one claims "I am possessed of virtues" even in the absence of [actual] virtues such as generosity and ethical discipline, one thereby accepts a state of possessing virtues that lacks a real basis; therefore, it is called a false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
Even if faults serve as its basis, since those [faults] are not virtues, there is indeed a lack of a real basis (*nirvastukatva*) in relation to virtues.
The phrase "due to the lack of a real basis" means "due to the lack of a foundation."
"What is view? he says: "Vision," and so forth.

Although the term "vision" is used here as a general designation, it nevertheless refers specifically to the five views beginning with the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because it is the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are under discussion here, and those [five] have the nature of afflictions.
However, mundane right view or the untainted (*anāsrava*) view is not included.
He asks, "What is the cause of this distinction among them? and answers with the words beginning "But of these," and so forth.

Even though there is no distinction between them in terms of their being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or their having the mode of thorough investigation (*nitīraṇākāra*), nevertheless, there is a mutual distinction due to the difference in their objects (*ālambana*) and the difference in their modes (*ākāra*).
Thorough investigation (*nitīraṇa*) means precise determination (*nirūpaṇa*).
"What is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)? To this he says: "In that regard, the view of a self-identity," and so forth.
That which is the vision of the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) in the form of a self or what belongs to a self is the view of a self-identity.
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) aggregates are called the aggregates of clinging.
"What is the view of grasping at extremes? To this he says: "The view of grasping at extremes," and so forth.

When the five aggregates of clinging have previously been apprehended as self and as belonging to a self, that subsequent vision which occurs in the form of annihilation or in the form of permanence is the view of grasping at extremes. A view preceded by grasping is a "view of grasping"; the meaning is that it is the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The view of grasping at extremes is the view of holding to the two extremes.
"What is wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi)? he asks, and says: "Wrong view," and so forth.

That view by which one denies the cause—characterized by giving, sacrifice, offerings, good conduct, and bad conduct—and denies the fruit of maturation—characterized by results in this world and the next—or denies the actions toward one's parents, or that which destroys existing reality such as the Arhats and others—that is called wrong view because it is the most sinful of all views.
What is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)? He says: "The adherence to views," and so forth.
That perception which regards the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as being foremost, distinguished, excellent, and supreme is the adherence to views.
It is called "foremost" because of its preeminence, and "distinguished" because it is superior to others.
It is the best because there is nothing superior to it; it is the highest because there is no other beyond it.
"What is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)? he asks, and says: "The adherence to rules and observances," and so forth.
That view which regards the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) as purity, liberation, and the means of deliverance is the adherence to rules and observances.
It is [regarded as] purity because it washes away the stain of evil; it is [regarded as] liberation because of the removal of the bondage of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is characterized by leading to liberation because it has the function of bringing about nirvāṇa.
"What is doubt? he asks, and says: "Doubt," and so forth.
Doubt is that state of indecision regarding actions, their fruits, the truths, and the jewels.
To demonstrate its etymology, he says: "Various cognitions," and so forth.
This is easily understood.
If "various-mindedness" (*vividhā matiḥ*) were indeed "doubt" (*vimatiḥ*), then it would follow that it is wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, he says: "If [it is] discerned," and so forth.
For wisdom has the nature of investigation (*pravicaya*).
But this [consciousness] proceeds in two ways; therefore, it is understood as being a different thing [from the other].

Establishing the connection with what is to be said hereafter, he says: "The six afflictions have been stated," and so forth. This has already been explained. Now, showing the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), he says:
Furthermore, there are anger and enmity;
hypocrisy, spite, envy, and avarice along with deceit;
guile, arrogance, lack of harm, shamelessness, lack of dread, lethargy, and restlessness.
Lack of faith, then laziness, heedlessness, and lost mindfulness;

distraction, lack of clear comprehension, regret, and even torpor; as well as applied thought and sustained thought—these secondary afflictions belong to the two [categories] and are of two kinds. 13–15.
And so forth. Regarding the phrase "in two ways for the two": there are two pairs, meaning two types;
thus, it is stated that there are four things of two kinds.
To the question "What is anger? he says: "In that regard, anger," and so forth.
That mental affliction (*cetasas āghātaḥ*) which arises based on a present injury is anger.
And this anger does not differ from hostility (*pratigha*), because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is that of hostility.
However, it is designated as such within a particular state of that very same hostility (*pratigha*).
And thus, in the recitation of the section on hostility, it is distinguished separately.
To the question "In what particular state is it designated?", he says: "present harm," and so forth.

As long as an injury has not been averted, that very malice of the mind which arises with respect to the domains of sentient and non-sentient beings is designated as "anger" (*krodha*), a specific form of malice.
Its function is to provide a basis for taking up sticks and so forth.
The phrase "with respect to the domains of sentient and non-sentient beings" means having living beings as its object and poison, weapons, thorns, and the like as its object.
By the term "taking up the staff" (*daṇḍādāna*), punishment is meant;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), execution, imprisonment, and so forth are included.
He asks, "What is malice? and says: "Malice," and so on.
"Following anger," and so forth. When anger has subsided, [one thinks]:

"This person has committed such an injury against me, who am of such a nature; shame on my life if I do not inflict a counter-injury upon him! I do not even bear the name of a human being. This persistence in the continuous activity of such a hostile disposition (*āśaya*) is *upanāha* (enmity).
Showing its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
Its function is to serve as the cause for intolerance (*akṣānti*).
Demonstrating intolerance, he says: "Intolerance is defined as the failure to endure harm and the desire for retaliation.
Demonstrating its status as a conceptual construct (*prajñaptisat*), he says: "This too," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
To the question "What is *mrakṣa* (concealment)? he says: "*Mrakṣa*, etc.
Explaining this, he says: "Out of desire, hatred, fear, and so forth," etc.

When one who reproves does not proceed with ill-will due to lack of faith and so forth, and when the one being reproved is a seeker of welfare, that person—having recognized the proper time for reproving and being a seeker of the other's welfare—reproves them, saying, "You have acted in such a way. When one who is thus reproved and questioned experiences a concealment of their fault arising from a portion of delusion (*moha*), that is called *mrakṣa* (concealment).
How is it a portion of delusion? To this he says: "But as for its being a portion of delusion," and so forth.
Because *mrakṣa* has the form of concealment, it is therefore a portion of delusion.
Showing his action, he says: "And this," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "This is the nature of things," and so forth.
This is the natural state of people or of phenomena: that remorse arises in a person who conceals their evil deed.
And remorse is necessarily associated with mental distress;
therefore, due to that association with mental distress, there arises a state of non-comfortable abiding.
"What is malice (*pradāśa*)? he asks, and says: "Malice," and so forth. Malice is the biting with fierce words.
To demonstrate what a fierce word is, he says: "Fierce by speech," and so forth.
That speech which is intensely harsh through the application of striking at the vital points (*marmaghaṭṭana*) is "fierce" (*caṇḍa*) speech.
"Intensely" (*pragāḍha*) means sharp.
Showing its biting nature, he says: "one who has the habit of biting," and so forth.
This mental factor has "biting" as its intrinsic nature; therefore, its state is "biting-ness" (*dāśitā*).
This abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used here in its own sense [to denote the quality].
Consequently, that very same mental factor, because it bites with fierce words, is designated by the term "fierce-word-biting-ness" (*caṇḍavacodāśitā*).
Showing that its existence is merely conceptual, he says, "And this," and so forth.
"Preceded by anger and enmity" means having anger and enmity as its cause.
The remainder is easily understood.
Showing its function, he says: "Of one who possesses that," and so forth.
Since suffering arises from dwelling together with a person who is prone to spite (*pradāśa*), therefore spite has as its function a state of non-comfortable abiding (*asparśavihāra*).
"What is envy (*īrṣyā*)? he asks, and says: "Envy," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "Of one who is intent upon gain and honor," and so forth.

When one who is attached to their own gain and honor perceives the gain and honor of others, as well as their specific virtues such as skillfulness and the like, there arises a mental state of resentment—a portion of hatred caused by intolerance—which is an outburst of anger; that is envy.
Showing its etymology, he says: "Its own basis," and so forth;
this is easily understood.
Showing its function, he says: "Dejection," and so forth.

Because it is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and because it results in an unpleasant state of existence (*asparśavihāra*) preceded by mental distress, it is said to have a dual function.
What is stinginess (*mātsarya*)? It is said: "Stinginess," and so forth.
That which is a grasping contrary to generosity is stinginess.
Demonstrating generosity, he says: "An appropriated object," and so forth.
He says: "Sloth," and so forth.
That lack of serviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) of the mind, which is its state of rigidity (*staimitya*), is sloth (*styāna*).
"What is this state of rigidity? To this he says: "The state of rigidity," and so forth. Rigidity (*staimitya*) is the state (*bhāva*) of that which is rigid (*stimita*).
The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) indicates the ground for the application of the term.
For it is thus: that connection by virtue of which the mind, due to its insentience, becomes stagnant and is unable to apprehend an object is called "stagnation" (*staimitya*).
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
"What is restlessness? he asks, and says: "Restlessness," and so forth.
That which is the non-quiescence of the mind is restlessness.
Why is this so? He says: "For quiescence," and so forth.
Because the term "quiescence" (*vyupaśama*) refers to calm abiding (*śamatha*), its opposite is "non-quiescence" (*avyupaśama*).

Furthermore, this non-quiescence is said to be "excitement" (*auddhatya*), because it is the cause of non-quiescence for a mind that recollects past laughter, play, sport, and so forth, which are conducive to passion.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "Its function is to obstruct calm abiding."
Śamatha is concentration; it is that which acts as an obscuration to it.
What is lack of faith? He says: "Lack of faith," and so forth.
Lack of faith is a state that is the opposite of faith, consisting of a lack of conviction regarding karma and other such matters.
To the question "From where does this [notion of] 'the adverse side' (vipakṣa) come?", he says: "For faith... and so forth.
This has already been explained.
"Lack of faith (aśraddhā) is its opposite," and so on.
This too is easily understood.
Showing the action [of the obstacle], he says: "Laziness," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "Of one who lacks faith," and so forth.

Since, as long as conviction and desire do not arise toward any form [of practice], so long does even the mere will for application (*chanda*) not arise; therefore, its function is to serve as the cause of laziness (*kausīdya*).
To the question "What is laziness?", he says: "Laziness," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "In regard to wholesome action of body, speech, and mind," and so forth.
The cause of this [laziness] is the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of reclining on one's side.
Even in one who is skilled in the defining statements and in physical activities and so forth, that lack of enthusiasm of the mind which arises as a portion of delusion is *kausīdya* (indolence).
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
It creates an obstruction to the application toward the side of the wholesome.
To the question "What is negligence? he says: "Negligence," and so forth.

Greed and the other factors by which one is seized such that one does not protect the mind from afflictions such as passion, nor practice the wholesome which serves as the antidote to passion and the rest—in these [factors], namely greed, delusion, and laziness, the designation "negligence" is applied.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
It functions as the cause for the increase of the unwholesome and the decrease of the wholesome. To the question "What is forgetfulness? he says: "Forgetfulness," and so forth;
it is that mindfulness which is associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Demonstrating the function [of distraction], he says: "And this," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
To the question "What is distraction?", he says: "Distraction," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "It is variously cast about," and so forth.
Mental distraction (*cittavikṣepa*) is that by which the mind is cast about upon an object in many ways.
Showing its existence as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisattva*), he says: "By those [defilements] such as passion, hatred, and delusion," and so forth.

Those passions such as attachment (*rāga*) by which the mind is led far away from the object of concentration (*samādhyālambana*), it is with respect to them that the designation "distraction" (*vikṣepaprajñapti*) is applied as appropriate.
Demonstrating its function, he says: "And this," etc.
It acts as an obscuration to dispassion (*vairāgya*), because one whose mind is distracted lacks dispassion.
"What is non-discernment (*asamprajanya*)? To this he says: "Non-discernment," and so forth. Non-discernment is said to be afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*).
Demonstrating what afflicted wisdom is, he says: "By which [wisdom] it is not cognized," and so forth.
That wisdom by which the conduct of body, speech, and mind remains unperceived during coming, going, and so forth, is called afflicted wisdom;
and that is lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*).
Demonstrating its function, he says: "that which is to be done," and so on.
By means of those [actions] that produce non-discernment, one does not reflect upon what is to be done and what is not to be done;
and consequently, his action becomes a cause for transgression.
"What is remorse (*kaukṛtya*)? he asks, and says: "Remorse," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "That which was done badly," and so forth.
When a thing that ought to be done in a certain way is instead done otherwise, then it is called "badly done" (*kukṛta*).
In that context, "kaukṛtya" refers to a contemptible action in its objective sense;
however, here, "kaukṛtya" refers to the mental distress or remorse regarding an ill-performed object,
because it is mental factors (*caitasika*) that are under discussion here.
Showing its function, he says: "And this," and so forth.
*Cittasthiti* (stability of mind) is *samādhi* (concentration). It creates an obscuration to that.
To the question "What is *middha* (torpor)? he says: "*Middha*," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "Functioning upon an object," and so forth.
That by virtue of which the mind proceeds toward an object without independence is called *middha* (torpor).
Providing another explanation for this very point, he says: "The sustaining of body and mind," and so forth.
That mental state by which the body is no longer sustained is *middha* (torpor), being that under whose influence one becomes lacking in self-control (*asvatantra*).
To demonstrate its contraction, he says: when the consciousnesses do not function through the doors of the sense-faculties such as the eye, that is their contraction.
By the inclusion of the term "lacking in self-control," he shows its distinction from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and by the term "contraction," its distinction from *styāna* (sloth).
Showing that this [self] exists only as a conceptual designation (prajñaptisattva), he says: "And this," and so forth.
This has already been explained. Showing its function (karman), he says: "The failure to perform what ought to be done," and so forth.
For one who is lying down, indeed, there is a loss of what ought to be done.
To the question "What is discursive thought (vitarka)? he says: "Discursive thought," and so forth.
That mental discourse (*manojalpa*) which consists of a specific kind of wisdom and volition, proceeding in the form of an investigation such as "What is this?", is discursive thought.
Showing that it is mental discourse (*manojalpa*), he says: "Of the mind," and so forth;
this is easily understood.
Showing the essential nature of discourse, he says: "Discourse is the verbal expression of meaning."

The meaning is that it is the expression of an object by means of the mind (*citta*). How does this [mind] have volition (*cetanā*) as its intrinsic nature? To this he says: "A particular kind of volition and wisdom" (*cetanā-prajñā-viśeṣa*), and so forth.

Since volition consists in the movement of the mind and wisdom functions in the form of discerning qualities and defects, and since the mind proceeds under the influence of these two, therefore, at times, *vitarka* (applied thought) is designated for both the mind and volition when nothing is being inferred; and at other times, it is designated for both wisdom and the mind when something is being inferred.
Providing another explanation on this very point, he says:
"The arising of the five [consciousnesses] in the root-consciousness occurs according to conditions."
Consciousness [arises] either together with or not together with [other consciousnesses], just as waves [arise] in water.
(15) Just as for visual consciousness the object is restricted to form alone, and for auditory consciousness it is restricted to sound alone, and so forth;
in this way, a specific immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is not asserted for visual consciousness and the others.
Since all six consciousnesses can, in turn, serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the arising of visual consciousness,
it must likewise be admitted that up to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), all six can serve as its immediately preceding condition in turn.
Consequently, even from a single immediately preceding condition, if an objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is present, the arising of two or many consciousnesses is not contradictory.

Now, if this is not accepted, then it must be asked: what is the reason here that, even though there is no restriction regarding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and even when the five [sense-objects] as objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*) are simultaneously present, consciousness arises through only one [of them] and not through all five?

Since no such restrictive cause whatsoever is observed in this case, therefore, given the existence of the objective conditions, either consciousness must arise for all five, or it must not arise for even one.
Introducing another point of discussion, he says: "This must now be stated," and so forth. The meaning of the question is easily understood.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says:
The arising of mental consciousness occurs at all times, except for the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika),
the two meditative attainments (samāpatti), torpor (middha), and fainting (mūrchana) which are without thought. 16, etc.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that, with the exception of those in the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exists at all times.
To demonstrate the meaning of the words, he says "at all times," and so forth;
this is easy to understand.
Regarding the point where the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not admitted, he says "of this general rule" (*asya utsargasya*), etc., while setting it aside.

Even though the existence of mental consciousness at all times has been accepted, nevertheless, its occurrence must be desired [only] excluding the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*), excluding the two attainments of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), excluding mindless sleep (*acittaka-middha*), and excluding mindless fainting (*acittikā-mūrchā*).
A general rule (*utsarga*) is said to be a prescription that applies when conditions are equal.
An exception (*apavāda*) is specifically prescribed.
Now, as to what this "state of non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*) is, he says: "In that regard, the state of non-perception," and so forth.
Certain gods are recited as being "beings without perception" (*asaṃjñisattva*).
The cessation of mind and mental factors for one who has been reborn among them is called the state of non-perception (āsaṃjñika).
"What are the two attainments? he asks, and says: "The two attainments," and so forth.
This is easy to understand.
"What is this attainment of non-perception? he asks, and says: "Therein, the attainment of non-perception," and so forth.

For a yogin who is free from passion regarding the third dhyāna, but not yet free from passion for what is above it, there occurs—preceded by the mental attention (manaskāra) characterized by the notion of liberation—the cessation of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) and of those mental factors (caitasika) associated with it; this is what is called "the attainment of non-perception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) in this teaching. To demonstrate its etymological derivation, he says: "by means of this, [consciousness] is ceased," and so forth.
This is a self-explanatory gloss.
