To the question "Who is such a person?", he says: "Furthermore, that [cessation] of the mental consciousness along with its associates," and so forth. That by which the activity of the mental consciousness together with its retinue is ceased is called "cessation.
And this is a certain particular state of the basis (*āśraya*), not a substantial entity (*dravya*) as it is imagined by some.

[Objection: But surely it is said that concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind that is wholesome and so forth; how then can the cessation of mind and mental factors be called an attainment (*samāpatti*)? [Response: He says, "from the attainment-mind," and so on.

Because immediately after the attainment-mind, a basis (*āśraya*) is obtained that is opposed to the arising of another mind, therefore that cessation of mind and mental factors is called an attainment.
Showing the second [type], he says: "The attainment of cessation," and so forth.

For a yogin who is free from passion regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), that cessation of the mental consciousness together with its attendants and of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*)—preceded by a mental attention consisting of the perception of a peaceful dwelling—is called the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"Preceded by the perception of a peaceful dwelling" means that having first formed the cognition, "This dwelling is peaceful," one subsequently enters into that attainment.
Showing that this [state] also exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisattva*), he says: "This too," and so forth.

The meaning is that just as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is designated as a particular state of the physical basis (*āśraya*), so too is this [attainment of sleep]. To the question of how sleep can be without consciousness (*acittaka*), he says: "Without consciousness," and so forth.

When the physical basis (*āśraya*) is impaired by intense torpor (*middha*), because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not function for that duration, it is therefore called "without mind" (*acittaka*). To the question, "How does a fainting fit (*mūrchā*) become 'without mind,' and how is it defined? he says: "Without mind," and so forth. If, due to an external injury or an imbalance of the bodily elements (*dhātu-vaiṣamya*), there occurs a disharmony of the physical basis caused by the temporary cessation of the activity of the mental consciousness, then upon that disharmony of the basis, a "fainting fit without mind" is metaphorically designated.
Having summarized [the topic], he says, showing it: "These very five states," and so forth.
The meaning of the summary is easy to understand.
Addressing the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), he asks and says: "In this way, in the case of the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) and so forth," and so on.
When the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) and so forth have passed away, from what then does that consciousness arise by which the yogin does not undergo death?
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) says: "That [consciousness] arises precisely from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)," and so on.
For one who has emerged from the state of non-perception and so forth, that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises from the storehouse-consciousness alone.

Because that storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is permeated by the seeds of all consciousnesses, [the author], establishing the connection with what is to be explained hereafter, says: "In which there is the transformation of consciousness," and so forth.
This is easily understood.

Regarding the proposition that the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) do not exist outside of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*), he now states [the following] in order to establish it:

"This transformation of consciousness is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); whatever is conceptually constructed by it does not exist. Therefore, all this is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). (17)
And so forth.
This transformation of consciousness is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Whatever object is conceptualized by that conceptual construction, none of it exists.
Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is that this entire world is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
To demonstrate the meaning of the individual components, he says "this which... and so forth;
the meaning of this is already explained.
Showing the essential nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he says: "Those whose forms are superimposed objects," and so forth.
Those minds and mental factors belonging to the three realms that function by way of a superimposed form are designated by the term "conceptual construction.
Regarding this, he cites the *Madhyāntavibhāga* as proof, saying: "As it has been stated," and so forth.
For it has been stated there [in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*] that "the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms are the imagination of the unreal" (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Why, then, is the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*) designated by the term "imagination" (*vikalpa*)? To this he says: "By that threefold," and so forth.

Since that entity—such as the receptacle world and so forth—which is conceptualized by this threefold transformation of consciousness (vijñānapariṇāma) along with its associated mental factors, does not exist in reality, therefore that transformation of consciousness is called "conceptualization" (vikalpa).
This is because its objective support (ālambana) does not exist as a real entity.
The proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin), unable to conceive of this, asks: "But how is this so? and so forth.
How is it known that the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpālambana*) does not exist as a real entity (*vastusat*)?
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "For that which is the cause of something," and so forth.
That which is accepted as the cause of something arises when that [cause] is complete.
And since it is not otherwise when there is no contradiction, this is the established principle:
consciousness arises even in the case of illusions and the like without an external object; therefore, we consider that the production of consciousness is not dependent upon an object.
Under the guise of a conclusion, [the author], demonstrating the cause of consciousness, says: "Therefore, from that preceding [consciousness] which has ceased," and so forth.
Since consciousness is thus not dependent upon an external object, consciousness arises precisely from a preceding consciousness of a similar form;
it does not arise from an external object, because that consciousness occurs even in the absence of an external object.
Thus, deficiency has first been demonstrated.
Now, demonstrating contradiction, he says: "And it is observed," and so forth.
Even with respect to an object of a single nature, mutually contradictory cognitions are observed among perceivers, such as in the forms of a corpse, a woman, or meat.
In this regard, it might be argued: "A single entity may indeed possess multiple forms.
To this he says: "And not for a single [entity]," and so forth.
For it is certainly not logical that a single object should possess mutually contradictory natures.
Since this is so, it should be understood that because the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses a superimposed form, its objective support (*ālambana*) is non-existent.
Demonstrating the conclusion, he says: "By this much," and so forth.
By stating the non-existence of the object of discourse, the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*) is avoided.
Now, wishing to avoid the objection up to its conclusion, he says: "Therefore, all this," and so forth.
Explaining this, he says: "By that" means "for that reason," and so forth.
Because whatever entity and so on is conceptualized by a conceptual construction whose nature is transformation, that does not exist in an ultimate sense.
But that conceptual construction (vikalpa) does exist.
Therefore, because of the non-existence of the object and the existence of conceptual construction, everything is representation-only (vijñaptimātra).
Showing the meaning of the individual parts, he says: "Everything," and so forth.
The meaning is that the term "all" (*sarva*) refers to the three realms (*traidhātuka*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for the word "mere" (*mātra*), it is for the purpose of excluding an object that exceeds [the mere] representation (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, the letter *ka* here does not signify "small," "short," "contemptible," or "praiseworthy."
Rather, it is for the purpose of completing the verse.
Anticipating the opportunity for another to raise an objection through recitation or inquiry, he says: "If all seeds," and so forth.

If everything, in its ultimate sense, is indeed representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and there exists no agent or instrument other than that representation-only, then it must be explained how various kinds of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) proceed from the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) without being presided over by an agent and without an instrument.
On this point, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says:
"For consciousness, which contains all seeds, undergoes transformation in such and such ways through mutual influence, whereby this or that conceptual construction (vikalpa) arises. (18)
And so forth.

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: the *ālayavijñāna* itself undergoes such a transformation through mutual force that those various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise, even without an agent or an instrument.
Showing the meaning of the individual components, the Commentator says: "In that regard, by the arising of all phenomena," and so forth.
Because the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is permeated by the capacities capable of producing all phenomena, it is therefore called "possessing all seeds" (*sarvabījaka*).
Demonstrating the purpose for employing these two qualifiers, he says: "For consciousness," and so forth.

Since there is also a consciousness called "evolving consciousness" (*pravṛttivijñāna*) which does not possess all seeds, this qualifier "possessing all seeds" was formulated in order to exclude that.

Some postulate that even apart from consciousness (*vijñāna*), there exists a primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or similar entity that contains all seeds; therefore, the term "consciousness" is employed in order to exclude that.
Providing another explanation for this very point, he says: "Or else, 'a single word' and so forth.

Just as in the case of "blue lotus," where there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified between two words, it is not so in every instance. Rather, in some cases, the relationship of qualifier and qualified occurs even when there is only one word, such as in "earth-substance" (*pṛthvī-dravya*).
For here, although water does not deviate from being a substance (*dravyatva*), it is nevertheless designated by the qualifier "substance.
Likewise, in this case as well, although all seeds do not deviate from being consciousnesses (*vijñānatva*), they are nevertheless qualified by the term "consciousness.
Intending to explain the meaning of the individual components [of the compound], he says: "transformation," and so forth.
Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the state of being distinct from its previous condition;
and that is characterized by the attainment of a state capable of producing that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) immediately thereafter.
The phrase "by mutual influence" is explained by the words "for thus," and so forth.

For when the visual and other consciousnesses proceed toward the nourishment of their own capacities, they then become the causal condition for the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as characterized by those capacities.
That transformation of the storehouse consciousness, in turn, becomes the causal condition for that visual and other consciousness.
Thus...
The latent impression of karma, together with the impression of the twofold grasping,
produces another maturation when the previous maturation has been exhausted. (19)
Whatever object is conceptualized by whichever conceptualization, that is merely the imagined nature; it does not exist. But the dependent nature is conceptualization, arising from conditions.
The perfected nature (niṣpanna-svabhāva) is its constant absence of that former [imagined nature].
For this very reason, it is neither different nor non-different from the dependent nature; it should be described like impermanence and so forth. When this is not perceived, the other is not seen.
Having in mind the threefold absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) of the threefold intrinsic nature, the absence of intrinsic nature of all phenomena was taught.
The first is indeed without intrinsic nature by its very characteristic; furthermore, the other...
The fact that this [nature] does not exist by itself is another form of the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā).

Since it is the ultimate reality (paramārtha) of all phenomena, it is also suchness (tathatā), because it remains as it is at all times; that very state is representation-only (vijñaptimātratā). 24–25.
As long as consciousness does not abide in the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātratva),
so long will the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the two-fold grasping (grāhadvaya) not cease.
For even the perception that "this is indeed representation-only" [is an obstacle].
Placing something before him, he does not abide in that alone.
But when consciousness no longer perceives an object at all,
then it abides in the state of mere consciousness, because in the absence of a graspable object, there is no grasping of it.
This is the absence of mind and non-apprehension; it is supramundane gnosis.
It is the revolution of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) through the twofold abandonment of depravity (dauṣṭhulya). // 29 //
This very outflow-free realm (anāsrava-dhātu) is inconceivable, wholesome, constant, blissful, and the body of liberation; it is this which is called the Dharma-body of the Great Sage.
Showing its twofold nature, he says: "In two ways," and so forth.
In this context, two kinds of *dauṣṭhulya* are intended: the *dauṣṭhulya* of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the *dauṣṭhulya* of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
To the question "What is *dauṣṭhulya*? he says: "*Dauṣṭhulya*, etc.
*Dauṣṭhulya* is said to be the unserviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) of the basis (*āśraya*).
Furthermore, in its ultimate sense, that *dauṣṭhulya* is called the seed of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Showing its divisions, he says: "That transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), moreover," and so forth.
One [type] is attained through the abandonment of the *dauṣṭhulya* belonging to the lineages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which is what is called the "body of liberation" (*vimuktikāya*).
The second [transformation] is attained through the abandonment of the dysfunctions (*dauṣṭhulya*) residing in the bodhisattva, as it is said: "This is the Dharma of the Great Sage.

Thus, it should be understood that here the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is described as being both with superior and without superior, distinguished by the abandonment of these two kinds of obscurations.
To provide proof for the demonstration of these two kinds of obscurations, he says: "In this regard, there is a verse," and so forth.
The appropriation-consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*), which has the nature of the two obscurations, is to be understood as bondage.
To the question "Of whom is there bondage?", he says: "Of the two.

The meaning is that by means of that storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), characterized as an obscuration, there is bondage for the two: namely, for those of the lineage of the śrāvakas and so forth, and for bodhisattvas.
By the statement "it contains all seeds" and "it is the seed of the afflictions," the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) are shown.

That *ālayavijñāna* which has these two obstructions as its characteristic is described in that way; that is, it is so called because within it—within the *ālayavijñāna*—there are all the seeds of the afflictions.
Showing the meaning of the individual parts, the author of the commentary says: "Of the two," and so forth.
For those belonging to the lineage of the śrāvakas and others, the seed of the afflictions is bondage;
for the bodhisattva, the seed of the two obstructions is bondage.
By the term "seed of the two obstructions," the "all-seed" (sarvabīja) is expressed.
Why is this an obscuration specifically for the bodhisattva? He says: "Because of its total eradication," and so forth.
Since omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is attained through the abandonment of these two types of obscurations, it is precisely that [omniscience] which is bound by this obscuration.
Having explained the verse, and wishing to explain the remainder of the subject matter previously introduced, he says: "That itself is untainted (*anāsrava*)," and so forth.
That very same specific transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) is called the untainted realm (anāsravo dhātuḥ).
Because it is free from all outflows (āsrava) due to its lack of depravity (nirdauṣṭhulya), it is "untainted" (anāsrava).
It is called a "realm" (dhātu) because it is the cause of all noble qualities (āryadharma); for here, the word *dhātu* is employed in the sense of "cause."
For all noble qualities (āryadharma) have that as their cause.
To the question "How is it inconceivable?", he says: "Inconceivable," and so forth.

Because it is not within the range of logic (tarka), because it is to be personally realized (pratyātmavedya) by the Noble Ones, and because there is no illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) for it, it is therefore inconceivable.
How is it wholesome? It is said: because its object is purity, because it is secure, and because it consists of untainted dharmas, it is therefore wholesome.
How is he "steadfast" (dhruva)? He says: because the Sugata is eternal and does not perish, therefore he is steadfast.
How is he "blissful" (sukha)? He says: "blissful," and so forth.
Because he is eternal, therefore he is blissful.
For that which is impermanent is suffering, but this [state] is permanent; therefore, it is bliss.

Showing the difference in the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) according to the distinction between types of persons, he says: "By the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions," and so forth.
That specific transformation of the basis is called the *vimuktikāya* (body of liberation) of the Śrāvakas.
Because for them only the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is abandoned,
they attain liberation by that much alone;
therefore, it is said that the basis of liberation is the "body of liberation" (*vimuktikāya*).
However, for the Great Sage, that very same state characterized by the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
For what reason is it said that this belongs to the Blessed One as his Dharma-body? He says: "By the cultivation of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*)," and so forth.

Because, through the cultivation of the stages and the perfections, there occurs the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, and the revolution of the basis is fully realized; therefore, it is called the Dharma-body of the Great Sage.
This is what is meant: because it is accumulated by means of the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*), it is therefore called the *dharmakāya*.
